clue: Four 65-foot statues of Ramesses II guard these temples, which were cut apart and moved uphill in the 1960s to escape a dam's rising lake.
fact: Twice a year the sun shines all the way into the inner sanctuary.

clue: The Rolling Stones and Paul McCartney recorded at AIR Studios on this island until a 1989 hurricane; a volcano later buried its capital in ash.
fact: Plymouth is the only ghost town in the world that is still officially a capital.

clue: The Lumière brothers filmed one of the first motion pictures, of workers leaving their factory, in this French city in 1895.
fact: It is often called France's food capital.

clue: Elvis Presley was born in a two-room house in this town on January 8, 1935.
fact: He got his first guitar at the town's hardware store, reportedly when he wanted a rifle.

clue: Mark Twain wrote Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn while living in a Victorian Gothic mansion in this city.
fact: Harriet Beecher Stowe lived next door.

clue: Maya pyramids here rise above the rainforest canopy; one appeared as a rebel base in the first Star Wars film.
fact: Temple IV is about 230 feet tall.

clue: The "Door of No Return" in a slave house on this small island off Africa's westernmost city became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade.
fact: Nelson Mandela and Barack Obama both visited the door.

clue: U.S. Marines fought block by block for nearly a month in 1968 to retake this old imperial capital's walled citadel.
fact: The Nguyen emperors ruled from its Imperial City until 1945.

clue: A giant glass dome holding an indoor desert is a star attraction at the Henry Doorly Zoo in this city.
fact: The Desert Dome is billed as the world's largest indoor desert.

clue: Theodore Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for brokering the 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War, signed at a navy yard here.
fact: The shipyard itself is actually across the river in Kittery, Maine.

clue: A white lighthouse standing on bare granite above a tiny fishing village near Halifax is said to be the most photographed in Canada.
fact: The lighthouse once housed a small post office.

clue: The 1648 peace that ended the Thirty Years' War was negotiated in this city and its neighbor Osnabrück.
fact: Historians often date the modern system of sovereign states to this peace.

clue: A gold rush made this mountain town one of the richest cities in the Americas in the 1700s; it was also the center of a failed independence plot led by "Tiradentes."
fact: Its name means "black gold," for gold coated in dark iron oxide.

clue: An August 2023 wildfire destroyed most of this historic whaling town, but its 150-year-old banyan tree survived.
fact: The town was the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom in the early 1800s.

clue: Boxer Muhammad Ali was born in this river city, where a museum and the airport carry his name.
fact: He took up boxing as a boy after his bike was stolen.

clue: Neon signs and street food fill the Dōtonbori canal district of this Japanese city, which hosted a World Expo in 2025.
fact: Locals are famous for takoyaki, octopus dumplings.

clue: Europe's oldest university, founded in 1088, is in this Italian city known for its miles of covered porticoes.
fact: Bolognese sauce is named for the city.

clue: More than 600 small bronze dwarf statues hide around this Polish city, a nod to an anti-communist protest group.
fact: Before 1945 it was the German city of Breslau.

clue: Gilded Age millionaires built enormous summer "cottages" like The Breakers along the Cliff Walk in this city.
fact: The Breakers was built for Cornelius Vanderbilt II and has 70 rooms.

clue: The highest peak east of the Mississippi River, at 6,684 feet, is named for a professor who died in a fall while measuring it.
fact: Elisha Mitchell is buried on the summit.

clue: More than 1,200 grassy, cone-shaped hills, which turn brown in the dry season, cover the countryside of this central Philippine island.
fact: Legend says they are the dried tears of a heartbroken giant.

clue: Siddhartha Gautama is said to have reached enlightenment under a fig tree here, which makes it the holiest site in Buddhism.
fact: The tree there today is said to descend from the original.

clue: A double ring of medieval walls with 52 towers encircles the hilltop old city of this town in southern France.
fact: Architect Viollet-le-Duc restored it in the 1800s, adding pointed slate roofs that critics called inaccurate.

clue: This theme park opened in 1971 on swampland outside a central city, with Cinderella Castle at its center.
answer: Magic Kingdom, Walt Disney World, Florida
fact: Walt Disney died in 1966 and never saw it open.

clue: A granite face in profile that looked out from a cliff here fell in 2003, but it remains on the state's license plates and quarter.
answer: Old Man of the Mountain, Franconia Notch, New Hampshire
fact: Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote a story about it, "The Great Stone Face."

clue: The Uros people live on floating islands they weave from reeds on the world's highest navigable lake.
fact: The lake sits about 12,500 feet above sea level.

clue: Bareback riders race around this Tuscan city's shell-shaped main square twice each summer in the Palio.
fact: A horse can win even if its rider has fallen off.

clue: A 2,000-year-old Roman aqueduct of granite blocks held together without mortar marches through this Spanish city.
fact: Its tallest arches reach about 93 feet.

clue: Nicknamed "Galloping Gertie," this suspension bridge twisted itself apart in a 42-mph wind just four months after opening in 1940.
fact: The only death was a cocker spaniel named Tubby, left in a car on the bridge.

clue: Part of the 12-story Champlain Towers South condominium collapsed in the middle of the night in June 2021 in this beach town.
fact: Ninety-eight people died in one of the deadliest building collapses in U.S. history.

clue: Long famous for holding steady while most of the world's glaciers shrank, this 19-mile ice river in Patagonia has started retreating fast since 2019, and visitors on walkways watch chunks crash from its 200-foot face into a lake.
fact: Every few years its front dams the lake until the ice wall bursts.

clue: A submersible carrying five people imploded in June 2023 while diving to this famous 1912 wreck.
fact: The wreck lies about 12,500 feet down and wasn't found until 1985.

clue: Donkeys still outnumber cars in this Swahili island town, lived in for about 700 years.
fact: It is the oldest continually lived-in Swahili town in East Africa.

clue: Sled-dog teams finish the 1,000-mile Iditarod race in this Bering Sea town, which got diphtheria serum by dog relay in 1925.
fact: Balto, the lead dog on the final leg, has a statue in New York's Central Park.

clue: A copper mine just outside Salt Lake City is more than 2.5 miles wide and about three-quarters of a mile deep, one of the largest man-made holes on Earth.
fact: It has produced more copper than any other mine in history.

clue: The first soccer World Cup final was played in 1930 at a stadium built for it in this capital, and the home team won.
fact: The home team beat Argentina 4–2 in the final.

clue: Canadian troops fighting together for the first time captured this ridge from the Germans in April 1917.
fact: France gave the land for the memorial to Canada forever.

clue: A temple in this hill city holds what is believed to be a tooth of the Buddha, carried in a famous yearly procession of elephants.
fact: It was the capital of the last independent Sinhalese kingdom until the British took it in 1815.

clue: Jazz great Louis Armstrong was born in this city in 1901, and its airport is named for him.
fact: Much of the city sits below sea level.

clue: Franklin Roosevelt was born on, and buried at, his family's estate on the Hudson River in this town.
fact: FDR's presidential library there was the first one in the U.S.

clue: The first Nazi concentration camp opened in this town outside Munich in March 1933.
fact: U.S. troops liberated the camp on April 29, 1945.

clue: Before becoming the first U.S.-born pope in 2025, Robert Prevost served as bishop of this city on the northern coast of an Andean country.
fact: He also became a citizen of the country where he served.

clue: About a third of the buildings in this Baltic capital's center are Art Nouveau, more than in any other city.
fact: It was a leading Hanseatic League city.

clue: The Ambassador Bridge, the busiest U.S.–Canada border crossing by value of trade, links this city to Windsor, Ontario.
fact: Windsor, Ontario, lies directly south of the city across the river.

clue: A secret Cold War bunker for all of Congress was hidden for 30 years beneath a luxury resort here.
answer: The Greenbrier, White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia
fact: Its existence was revealed by the Washington Post in 1992.

clue: Mariachi music was born in the region around this western Mexican city, not far from the town that gave tequila its name.
fact: It is one of Mexico's three largest cities.

clue: Sweden's King Gustavus Adolphus was killed in 1632 leading a cavalry charge in fog here, though his army won.
fact: A memorial chapel marks the spot where he fell.

clue: Giant pandas are bred at a famous research base on the edge of this Sichuan city, known for spicy food.
fact: Sichuan peppercorns make the mouth tingle.

clue: The 6.7-magnitude earthquake that struck before dawn on January 17, 1994, collapsing freeways and an apartment building, is named for this San Fernando Valley neighborhood.
fact: The epicenter was actually in neighboring Reseda. It is one of the costliest natural disasters in U.S. history.

clue: A French immigrant family started a gunpowder mill on the Brandywine River here in 1802; it grew into a chemical giant.
fact: The original mills are now the Hagley Museum.

clue: Millions of tons of sand were dredged from the Gulf floor to build an island shaped like a palm tree off this city.
fact: No concrete or steel went into the island's base, only sand and rock.

clue: A church council here ended the Great Schism with a single pope in 1417, but first burned the reformer Jan Hus at the stake.
fact: It is the only papal election ever held north of the Alps.

clue: Golden fish-like creatures called shachihoko top the castle of this Japanese city, in Toyota's home region.
fact: It sits between Tokyo and Osaka on the bullet-train line.

clue: MLK DAY: Martin Luther King Jr. was shot on the balcony of this motel on April 4, 1968; it is now a civil rights museum.
fact: He had given his "I've Been to the Mountaintop" speech the night before.

clue: MLK DAY: Linda Brown's father sued this city's school board, leading to the 1954 Supreme Court ruling that ended legal school segregation.
fact: Her all-Black school, Monroe Elementary, is now a national historical park.

clue: MLK DAY: British soldiers shot 26 unarmed civil rights marchers in this city on January 30, 1972, killing 13 that day; the day is called Bloody Sunday.
fact: A 2010 government inquiry found the killings were "unjustified and unjustifiable."

clue: MLK DAY: Gandhi, King's great inspiration, finished his 240-mile Salt March by picking up salt on the beach at this village in 1930.
fact: About 60,000 Indians were jailed in the protests that followed.

clue: MLK DAY: Police fired on a crowd protesting pass laws in this township in March 1960, killing 69; the date is now a human rights holiday.
fact: The government banned the ANC soon afterward.

clue: Covered wooden bridges in this county inspired a 1990s bestselling romance novel, and John Wayne was born in its county seat.
fact: Clint Eastwood and Meryl Streep starred in the 1995 film.

clue: A 3-mile boardwalk known for Thrasher's French fries and saltwater taffy runs along the Atlantic in this Maryland resort city.
fact: A 1933 hurricane cut the inlet that separates it from the barrier island to the south.

clue: Nearly every English monarch since William the Conqueror has been crowned in this Gothic church.
fact: Charles Darwin and Isaac Newton are buried there.

clue: Lord Byron died of fever in this town in 1824 while helping the Greeks fight for independence.
fact: Byron is still a national hero in Greece; many boys there were named "Vyron" after him.

clue: Nineteen 18th-century windmills line the drainage canals of this village outside Rotterdam.
fact: They were built to pump water off land that lies below sea level.

clue: The Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass in this park on the Canadian border.
answer: Logan Pass, Glacier National Park, Montana
fact: The park had about 150 glaciers in 1850; only a couple dozen remain.

clue: The world's first chairlifts were installed at this ski resort in 1936, adapted from equipment for loading bananas onto ships.
fact: Ernest Hemingway lived nearby and is buried in Ketchum.

clue: Velázquez's Las Meninas and Goya's "black paintings" hang in this capital's great art museum.
fact: The museum opened in 1819.

clue: Marlborough and Prince Eugene beat the French and Bavarians here in 1704; a famous English palace is named for the battle.
fact: Winston Churchill was born at Blenheim Palace.

clue: One of Africa's busiest ports is in this Indian Ocean city, home to one of the largest Indian communities outside India.
fact: Gandhi spent years as a lawyer in its province.

clue: The Colorado River carved this mile-deep gorge; most visitors see it from the historic lodges and lookouts of this village on its South Rim.
fact: The rocks at the bottom are nearly 2 billion years old.

clue: Amelia Earhart was born in this Missouri River town in 1897.
fact: Her birthplace home on the river bluff is now a museum.

clue: A 16th-century Spanish fortress called El Morro guards the entrance to this old city's harbor.
fact: The fort's walls are up to 18 feet thick.

clue: Nearly 1,000 giant stone heads called moai stand on this remote island.
fact: Many moai have bodies buried underground beneath the heads.

clue: A mosque and an Orthodox cathedral stand side by side inside the white-walled kremlin of this city on the Volga, capital of Tatarstan.
fact: Ivan the Terrible captured it in 1552.

clue: This Texas city sits across the Rio Grande from Ciudad Juárez, and together they form one of the largest cross-border metro areas in the world.
fact: Unlike most of Texas, it is in the Mountain time zone.

clue: Thousands of Confederate prisoners were held at a five-sided granite fort on Pea Patch Island in this state's river.
fact: Reenactors at the fort today play prisoners, guards and blacksmiths.

clue: Hot springs have built white travertine terraces down a hillside in western Turkey, above the ruins of the Roman spa city Hierapolis.
fact: The name means "cotton castle."

clue: Napoleon III surrendered with more than 100,000 men after this battle in September 1870; Paris declared a republic two days later.
fact: It is also home to one of the largest fortified castles in Europe.

clue: The highest mountain outside Asia, about 22,800 feet tall, rises in the Andes on Argentina's side of the border with Chile.
fact: Climbers can reach the top by its normal route without technical gear.

clue: A 37-foot left-field wall called the Green Monster stands in this ballpark, the oldest in the major leagues, opened in 1912.
fact: One seat painted red marks the landing spot of Ted Williams's longest home run there.

clue: German Pietists built seven villages in eastern Iowa in the 1850s and ran them as a commune until 1932; the name now appears on refrigerators.
fact: The appliance company started in one of the villages in 1934 and took the colonies' name.

clue: A bronze Buddha about 50 feet tall sits inside a huge wooden temple hall here, and tame deer roam the park outside.
fact: Visitors try to squeeze through a hole in a pillar that is the same size as the Buddha's nostril.

clue: The Ottomans crushed the Hungarian army here in 1526; the young King Louis II drowned while fleeing.
fact: Hungarians still say "more was lost at Mohács" when something goes badly.

clue: A 325-foot golden stupa, said to hold strands of the Buddha's hair, towers over Myanmar's largest city.
fact: Its top is set with thousands of diamonds and rubies.

clue: A container ship lost power and slammed into this bridge in March 2024, collapsing it into the Patapsco River.
fact: The bridge was named for the author of "The Star-Spangled Banner."

clue: William Faulkner wrote at Rowan Oak in this college town, the model for Jefferson in his fictional Yoknapatawpha County.
fact: Faulkner wrote an outline of one novel on his study wall.

clue: Its hilltop old town, the Pelourinho, is full of colonial churches and the African-rooted culture of Brazil's first capital.
fact: It was the capital of colonial Brazil until 1763.

clue: Thirty-three miners trapped half a mile underground for 69 days were pulled up one by one in a capsule at a copper and gold mine here in 2010.
fact: Over a billion people watched the rescue on TV.

clue: The largest ancient religious complex in the world, with a hall of 134 giant columns, stands on the Nile's east bank in this Egyptian city.
fact: An avenue of sphinxes once ran almost two miles from it to another temple.

clue: Its jagged granite peaks rise about 7,000 feet straight up from the valley floor with no foothills, above a famous ski town's valley.
fact: The Grand Teton reaches 13,775 feet.

clue: After fleeing Austria, the singing family from The Sound of Music settled in this ski town and opened a lodge.
fact: Maria von Trapp is buried in the family cemetery there.

clue: A perfectly round sinkhole about 1,000 feet across and over 400 feet deep sits in the middle of a coral reef here.
fact: Jacques Cousteau made it famous in 1971.

clue: Simón Bolívar died of tuberculosis at a sugar estate outside this port city on South America's Caribbean coast in 1830.
fact: It is one of the oldest surviving Spanish cities in South America, founded in 1525.

clue: Women free divers called haenyeo, some in their 80s, put on shows below this crater-topped volcanic cone that rises from the sea at the east end of a Korean island.
fact: Visitors climb it at dawn to watch the sunrise.

clue: Father Flanagan founded a home for orphan boys here in 1917; it became its own village with its own post office.
fact: Spencer Tracy won an Oscar playing Father Flanagan in 1938.

clue: The world's largest children's museum is in this state capital.
fact: Life-size dinosaurs appear to be breaking out of its walls.

clue: Freddie Mercury was born in Stone Town on this spice island, which also lost the shortest war in history, about 40 minutes, in 1896.
fact: It joined Tanganyika in 1964 to form Tanzania.

clue: Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of this volcano is the farthest point from Earth's center.
fact: It is about 1.3 miles farther from Earth's center than the top of Everest.

clue: A whisper on the stage of this 4th-century BC theater, built for a healing sanctuary of Asclepius, can be heard in the top rows.
fact: It still hosts plays every summer.

clue: A country singer opened her own theme park in 1986 in the Smoky Mountain foothills near her hometown.
fact: Her Imagination Library has mailed more than 200 million free books to children.

clue: This state's 21-story Art Deco capitol, built in the 1930s, is nicknamed "the Skyscraper of the Prairie."
fact: It replaced an earlier capitol that burned in 1930.

clue: A king built a palace on top of a 600-foot rock column in the center of this island nation off India's southern tip, entered through the paws of a giant stone lion.
fact: Ancient visitors scratched poems onto its "Mirror Wall."

clue: A Bahá'í house of worship shaped like a white lotus flower opened in 1986 in India's capital.
fact: Its 27 marble "petals" are arranged in clusters of three.

clue: A fortified clay village on an old caravan route at the edge of Morocco's Sahara has appeared in Gladiator and Game of Thrones.
fact: Only a few families still live inside the old walls.

clue: Joe Biden was born in this coal city, also the setting of TV's "The Office."
fact: It was nicknamed the "Electric City" for its early electric streetcars.

clue: More antebellum mansions survive in this Mississippi River bluff city than anywhere else in the South; it marks one end of a famous old trace.
fact: Before the Civil War it reportedly had more millionaires per person than any other U.S. city.

clue: The capital of the world's lowest-lying country sits on an island in the Indian Ocean barely 3 feet above sea level.
fact: The government once held a cabinet meeting underwater to draw attention to rising seas.

clue: Mutineers from HMS Bounty hid on this tiny island in the remote South Pacific, far southeast of Tahiti, and some of their descendants still live there.
fact: Fewer than 50 people live there, making it one of the least-populated territories in the world.

clue: This capital faces another country's capital across the Congo River, the closest pair of national capitals in the world apart from Rome and Vatican City.
fact: It is the largest French-speaking city in the world.

clue: Twenty-seven giant radio dishes arranged in a Y on the Plains of San Agustin appeared in the movie Contact.
fact: The dishes move on railroad tracks to change the array's layout.

clue: Arbor Day was invented by a newspaper editor in this Missouri River town in eastern Nebraska in 1872; about a million trees were planted that first day.
fact: The founder, J. Sterling Morton, later became U.S. Secretary of Agriculture.

clue: Pastel houses crowd a narrow strip between a lake and steep mountains in this salt-mining village, often said to be one of the most photographed in the world.
fact: China built a full-size copy of the village in Guangdong.

clue: Leather has been dyed in stone vats of colored liquid at this medina's tanneries for centuries; it also claims the world's oldest university.
fact: Al-Qarawiyyin University was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, in 859.

clue: J.R.R. Tolkien grew up in this English city, which has more miles of canals than Venice.
fact: It was a center of the Industrial Revolution.

clue: A 235-foot sea stack called Haystack Rock towers over the beach in this town, which appears in the movie The Goonies.
fact: Puffins nest on the rock in spring and summer.

clue: Klondike gold rush stampeders landed at this boomtown in 1897 and hauled their gear over the White Pass.
fact: Con man Soapy Smith ran the town until he was shot in 1898.

clue: The world's southernmost national capital is also one of its windiest cities.
fact: Its parliament building is nicknamed "the Beehive."

clue: Montgomery's Eighth Army beat Rommel at this railway stop in late 1942; Churchill said before it Britain never had a victory, and after it never a defeat.
fact: Allied troops also used decoy tanks made of wood and canvas.

clue: A shroud some believe wrapped Jesus's body is kept in this city's cathedral; Fiat was founded here too.
fact: It hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.

clue: A pair of 60-foot bronze praying hands stands at the entrance of Oral Roberts University in this oil city.
fact: Route 66 runs through the city.

clue: The Russian flag came down on Castle Hill here in October 1867 when the United States took over the territory.
fact: Critics called the purchase "Seward's Folly."

clue: Electric workers found a giant stone disk of a moon goddess in 1978, leading to the excavation of an Aztec great temple in this city.
fact: The Spanish built their cathedral partly out of the temple's stones.

clue: Douglas MacArthur landed troops behind North Korean lines at this port in September 1950, despite tides of more than 30 feet.
fact: Seoul's main international airport is there today.

clue: A mountain striped red, yellow and turquoise by minerals rises about 17,000 feet in the Andes near Cusco.
fact: It became famous only in the 2010s, after its snow cover melted away.

clue: A wooden roller coaster called the Cyclone has thrilled riders at this Brooklyn beach amusement area since 1927.
fact: Nathan's hot dog eating contest is held there every Fourth of July.

clue: Two presidents named Bush spent summers at the family's oceanfront compound at Walker's Point in this town.
fact: George H.W. Bush went skydiving there for his 85th birthday.

clue: Only the stone front survives of a 17th-century Jesuit church in this former Portuguese colony, now gambling's world capital.
fact: Portugal handed the territory to China in 1999.

clue: A great stepped ziggurat built around 2100 BC still stands at this Sumerian city, said to be Abraham's birthplace.
fact: Leonard Woolley's dig there in the 1920s found royal tombs full of gold.

clue: Leonhard Euler proved no walk could cross each of this city's seven bridges exactly once; philosopher Immanuel Kant was born, taught and died here.
fact: The puzzle helped found graph theory.

clue: Abraham Lincoln practiced law and lived in this state capital, and he is buried in a tomb here.
fact: Lincoln's home there is the only house he ever owned.

clue: Bob Dylan grew up in this iron-mining town near the Hull–Rust pit, one of the world's largest open iron mines.
fact: Greyhound Lines started there in 1914 hauling miners.

clue: A skyscraper topped by a giant steel arch, nicknamed the "bottle opener," rises over Saudi Arabia's capital.
fact: The city's name comes from an Arabic word for gardens.

clue: Gabriel García Márquez was born in this banana-region town near South America's Caribbean coast, the model for Macondo in One Hundred Years of Solitude.
fact: García Márquez won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.

clue: Shackleton's stranded crew waited more than four months on this barren island in 1916 while he sailed 800 miles for help.
fact: All 22 men left behind there survived.

clue: Domino players and cigar rollers fill Calle Ocho in this Cuban-American neighborhood.
fact: Its Domino Park was officially named for Máximo Gómez.

clue: On one day each October, BASE jumpers leap legally from this 876-foot-high steel arch bridge in southern West Virginia.
answer: New River Gorge Bridge, West Virginia
fact: It was the longest single-span arch bridge in the world when it opened in 1977.

clue: FIFA, soccer's world governing body, has its headquarters in this Swiss banking city on a lake.
fact: Its main shopping street, the Bahnhofstrasse, is said to sit above bank vaults full of gold.

clue: Napoleon ruled this small island for about 10 months in 1814–15 before escaping to start the Hundred Days.
fact: He got 1,000 soldiers and a small navy as "emperor" of the island.

clue: Finished in 1970 with Soviet help, this dam on the upper Nile in southern Egypt created one of the world's largest artificial lakes.
fact: It ended the Nile's yearly floods.

clue: The USS Midway aircraft-carrier museum and a famous zoo in Balboa Park draw visitors to this Navy city near the Mexican border.
fact: The zoo was a pioneer of open-air, cage-free exhibits.

clue: Folk singer Woody Guthrie, who wrote "This Land Is Your Land," was born in this town in 1912.
fact: His guitar carried the slogan "This machine kills fascists."

clue: The country this Central American capital leads abolished its army in 1948.
fact: Its National Theatre was paid for with a tax on coffee exports.

clue: Red sandstone ruins of a Jesuit mission town, one of many where Guaraní people lived in the 1600s and 1700s, stand in the subtropical forest of South America's interior here.
fact: The 1986 film The Mission is set in these Jesuit missions.

clue: Its fortress overlooks the spot where the Sava flows into the Danube, and Tito is buried in this capital.
fact: It has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times.

clue: Street names on the original Monopoly board come from this seaside resort famous for its boardwalk.
fact: Marvin Gardens on the board is misspelled; the real place is Marven Gardens.

clue: More than 10,000 Japanese Americans were held during World War II at a camp below a tall butte near Cody here.
fact: Future Secretary of Transportation Norman Mineta was held there as a boy.

clue: A tiny island with a church sits in the middle of this Alpine lake below a cliffside castle.
fact: Ringing the church's "wishing bell" is said to make your wish come true.

clue: Charlemagne made this hot-springs city his capital, and German kings were crowned in his chapel here for 600 years.
fact: Charlemagne's throne is still in the cathedral.

clue: The main castle of the Ryukyu Kingdom stood on a hill here; fire destroyed its rebuilt main hall in 2019.
fact: The Ryukyu Kingdom paid tribute to China and Japan at the same time.

clue: LUNAR NEW YEAR: The oldest Chinatown in North America, entered through the Dragon Gate on Grant Avenue, holds one of the biggest Lunar New Year parades outside Asia.
fact: The parade's Golden Dragon is more than 200 feet long.

clue: LUNAR NEW YEAR: Chinese immigrants were held here for weeks or months under the Exclusion Act, and some carved poems into the barracks walls.
fact: The station operated from 1910 to 1940.

clue: LUNAR NEW YEAR: Ming and Qing emperors prayed for good harvests at the round, triple-roofed hall of this temple complex.
fact: The hall was built without a single nail.

clue: LUNAR NEW YEAR: Full-size buildings carved from blocks of river ice light up every winter at a festival in this city in China's far northeast.
fact: Winter temperatures there often drop below −20°F.

clue: LUNAR NEW YEAR: Thousands of paper sky lanterns are released at the Lantern Festival in this old mining district in the hills east of Taipei, the final night of the New Year season.
fact: People write wishes on the lanterns before letting them go.

clue: A garden built in 1932 straddles the border with Canada, with a cairn marking the line between two countries.
fact: Visitors can walk across the border inside the garden without a checkpoint, though they must clear customs when they leave.

clue: Called the "Niagara of the West," this 212-foot waterfall on the Snake River in southern Idaho is taller than Niagara.
fact: Evel Knievel tried to jump the nearby Snake River Canyon on a rocket in 1974.

clue: Almost every building in the old medina of this town in Morocco's Rif Mountains is washed in shades of blue.
fact: Jewish refugees who settled there in the 1930s are often credited with starting the blue paint tradition.

clue: Britain sent its worst repeat convicts to a prison settlement on this peninsula southeast of Hobart, Tasmania from 1830 to 1877.
fact: Its "Separate Prison" kept inmates in total silence.

clue: Heinrich Schliemann dug up a gold funeral mask here in 1876 and reportedly declared he had "gazed on the face of Agamemnon."
fact: The mask is now thought to be several centuries older than the Trojan War.

clue: A full-size replica of the Parthenon, built for an 1897 expo, stands in this city's Centennial Park with a 42-foot Athena inside.
fact: The Athena statue is covered in more than 8 pounds of gold leaf.

clue: Recruits from the eastern U.S., along with most female Marine recruits, have gone through boot camp on this Sea Island since 1915.
fact: It is one of only two Marine recruit depots in the country.

clue: A white-domed basilica sits on top of this artists' hill, once home to Picasso and Van Gogh.
fact: The basilica's white stone cleans itself when it rains.

clue: A 1902 eruption of this volcano wiped out the town of Saint-Pierre in minutes; one of the few survivors was a prisoner in a thick-walled cell.
fact: The survivor, Ludger Sylbaris, later toured with Barnum & Bailey's circus.

clue: The ornate mausoleum of shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, home of the carved "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" monkeys, stands in this mountain town north of Tokyo.
fact: Its buildings are decorated with about 2.4 million sheets of gold leaf.

clue: MARDI GRAS: The oldest Mardi Gras in the United States has been held in this Gulf Coast city since the early 1700s.
fact: Parade riders there throw MoonPies.

clue: MARDI GRAS: In the Cajun Courir de Mardi Gras, masked riders go from farm to farm begging ingredients for gumbo and chasing live chickens around this town.
fact: Riders wear pointed hats called capuchons that make fun of the rich.

clue: MARDI GRAS: Samba schools parade before tens of thousands in a purpose-built stadium here during Carnival.
fact: The Sambadrome was designed by Oscar Niemeyer, the architect of Brasília.

clue: MARDI GRAS: Steel drums were invented in this city on the island of Trinidad, whose Carnival climaxes with costumed bands parading on Monday and Tuesday.
fact: The steelpan was first made from oil drums.

clue: MARDI GRAS: Men called Gilles in wax masks and ostrich-feather hats throw oranges into the crowd at this town's carnival in Belgium's French-speaking south, a UNESCO-listed tradition.
fact: Being a Gille is a tradition reserved for local men.

clue: An extinct volcanic crater looms over the hotels and surfers of Waikiki here.
fact: British sailors mistook calcite crystals on its slopes for diamonds.

clue: Wernher von Braun's team designed the Saturn V rocket in this city, now home to Space Camp.
fact: A real Saturn V is displayed lying down at the space center there.

clue: About 800,000 people were killed in 100 days in 1994; a memorial in this capital holds the remains of about 250,000 of them.
fact: The city is known now for a monthly community clean-up day, umuganda.

clue: Earthquakes ruined this colonial capital in 1773, so the government moved; its baroque ruins below three volcanoes became a UNESCO town.
fact: Its Holy Week processions walk over carpets made of colored sawdust and flowers.

clue: John Hanning Speke announced in 1862 that he had found the source of the Nile where it leaves Lake Victoria here.
fact: Some of Gandhi's ashes were scattered in the river there.

clue: Murals made of thousands of ears of colored corn on this building are redone every year.
fact: Its domes and minarets were added in 1937.

clue: Samuel Slater built America's first successful water-powered cotton mill here in 1793 using designs he memorized in England.
fact: In England he was called "Slater the Traitor."

clue: Christians believe Jesus was crucified and buried at the spot now inside this church, shared by several denominations.
answer: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
fact: For centuries a Muslim family has held the key to its front door.

clue: The Catholic Counter-Reformation was shaped by a church council held in this Alpine city on and off from 1545 to 1563.
fact: The council created seminaries to train priests.

clue: The Dutch East India Company ran its Asian empire from this port, founded in 1619 on the ruins of Jayakarta.
fact: Batavia's old town hall is now a history museum.

clue: A governor stood in the doorway of a building on this campus in 1963 to try to block two Black students from enrolling.
fact: One of the students, Vivian Malone, became the university's first Black graduate.

clue: Opponents of slavery's spread met in a one-room schoolhouse in this town in east-central Wisconsin in 1854 and helped found the Republican Party.
fact: The Little White Schoolhouse is now a National Historic Landmark.

clue: Claude Monet painted the water lilies in his garden pond in this village again and again over the last 30 years of his life.
fact: Monet had the Japanese-style footbridge over the pond painted green.

clue: About 200 Polish soldiers on this peninsula held out for a week after a German battleship opened fire on September 1, 1939.
fact: The battleship was the Schleswig-Holstein, on a "courtesy visit."

clue: Paella was born in the rice fields around this Spanish port, which also hosts the Las Fallas festival of burning giant figures.
fact: Its cathedral holds a cup claimed to be the Holy Grail.

clue: Prince recorded and lived at a complex called Paisley Park in this suburb.
fact: Paisley Park is now a museum.

clue: A 1920 shootout in this coal town during a miners' strike was part of the run-up to the Battle of Blair Mountain.
fact: The town sits across the Tug Fork from Kentucky, Hatfield-McCoy feud country.

clue: India's "Silicon Valley," a tech hub in the south of the country, is also known as the Garden City.
fact: At about 3,000 feet up, it has a milder climate than most Indian cities.

clue: Students and citizens rose up against military rule in this city in May 1980, and troops killed hundreds.
fact: Novelist Han Kang, who wrote about the uprising, won the Nobel Prize in 2024.

clue: This mountain capital's country has two heads of state: the president of France and a Catalan bishop.
fact: The country has no airport.

clue: VALENTINE'S DAY: Seven men were lined up against a garage wall and shot here on February 14, 1929, in a gangland killing blamed on Al Capone.
answer: St. Valentine's Day Massacre site, Chicago
fact: The garage was torn down in 1967.

clue: VALENTINE'S DAY: Volunteers in this self-styled "Sweetheart City" on Colorado's Front Range, north of Denver, re-mail thousands of valentines every February.
fact: The program started in 1947.

clue: VALENTINE'S DAY: Couples put so many "love locks" on this footbridge's railings that a section collapsed in 2014.
fact: The city removed about 45 tons of locks in 2015.

clue: VALENTINE'S DAY: English couples eloped across the border to marry at the blacksmith's shop in this village, because the next country's marriage laws were looser.
fact: Couples there could marry at 16 without parental consent.

clue: VALENTINE'S DAY: A basilica in this city in central Italy's Umbria holds the relics of a bishop named Valentine, martyred in the 3rd century.
fact: Terni holds a month of Valentine's events every February.

clue: PRESIDENTS' DAY: British troops set fire to this president's house in August 1814, during the War of 1812.
fact: Dolley Madison saved a portrait of George Washington before the British arrived.

clue: PRESIDENTS' DAY: This town was the birthplace of two presidents, a father and son, who are both buried in the same church.
fact: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson died on the same day: July 4, 1826.

clue: PRESIDENTS' DAY: Theodore Roosevelt and his Rough Riders charged up San Juan Heights in 1898 outside this city.
fact: Roosevelt got the Medal of Honor in 2001, more than 80 years after his death.

clue: PRESIDENTS' DAY: A 19-year-old George Washington made his only trip abroad to this easternmost island of the Caribbean in 1751, where he caught smallpox.
fact: Surviving smallpox there made him immune when it hit his army later.

clue: PRESIDENTS' DAY: Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev nearly agreed to scrap all their nuclear weapons at a white waterfront house in this capital in 1986.
fact: The house is said to be haunted.

clue: Old casino signs are displayed in a "boneyard" at the Neon Museum in this city.
fact: The first resort on what became the Strip opened in 1941.

clue: This state capitol is the only one in the U.S. with oil wells drilled on its grounds.
fact: One well, nicknamed "Petunia No. 1" because it was drilled in a flower bed, pumped oil until 1986.

clue: Each spring about 7 million flower bulbs bloom in these gardens in the heart of a country's tulip fields.
fact: During 1630s "tulip mania" a single bulb could sell for more than a house.

clue: Mussolini's army looted one of this city's ancient granite obelisks in 1937; Italy returned it in 2005.
fact: The kingdom of Aksum was one of the first states to adopt Christianity, in the 300s.

clue: Engineers in this Baltic capital wrote the software behind Skype, launched in 2003.
fact: Its medieval old town is among the best preserved in Europe.

clue: Cuban immigrants hand-rolled cigars in the brick factories of this Tampa neighborhood.
fact: José Martí gave speeches to cigar workers there to raise support for Cuban independence.

clue: Roger Williams founded this city in 1636 as a refuge for religious freedom after he was banished from Massachusetts.
fact: He named it in thanks for God's providence.

clue: Ottoman sultans ruled from this palace on a point above the Bosphorus for about 400 years; its harem had hundreds of rooms.
fact: Its treasury holds the Spoonmaker's Diamond, one of the largest in the world.

clue: A giant relief map of its whole country, built in 1905, is a park attraction in this Central American capital.
fact: It is Central America's largest city.

clue: Henry Ford built an American-style company town in the jungle here in 1928 to grow rubber, and it failed.
fact: Workers rioted over rules like forced American food and a ban on alcohol.

clue: Ivy-covered outfield walls surround the field at this North Side ballpark, home of the team that won the 2016 World Series.
fact: It didn't install lights for night games until 1988.

clue: The smallest state capital in the U.S. by population is also the only one without a McDonald's.
fact: Its gold-domed statehouse is topped by a statue of Ceres, the goddess of agriculture.

clue: Colorful colonial houses fill the old walled city of this Caribbean port, which Spanish treasure fleets once used.
fact: Its fortress, San Felipe de Barajas, was the largest Spain built in the Americas.

clue: Cavalry charged a crowd of 60,000 demanding voting reform in St. Peter's Field here in 1819, killing about 15.
fact: The name was a sarcastic play on Waterloo, fought four years earlier.

clue: Leaders of 29 Asian and African countries met at this city's conference in 1955 and laid the groundwork for the Non-Aligned Movement.
fact: China's Zhou Enlai and India's Nehru were among those attending.

clue: About 60 miles of wide sandy beach called the Grand Strand center on this resort city.
fact: It has around 80 golf courses nearby.

clue: Scientists have uncovered the bones of more than 60 Columbian and woolly mammoths trapped in an ancient sinkhole here, at the southern edge of South Dakota's Black Hills.
answer: Mammoth Site, Hot Springs, South Dakota
fact: Construction workers found it by accident in 1974.

clue: Granite "horns" and towers rise above blue glacial lakes in this Patagonian national park.
fact: The towers are about 12 million years old.

clue: British paratroopers held one end of this bridge on the Rhine for days in 1944, but Operation Market Garden failed here.
fact: The battle inspired the book and movie A Bridge Too Far.

clue: Alexander the Great crossed the desert to consult an oracle of Amun in this oasis in Egypt's Western Desert, near the Libyan border, which reportedly hailed him as a god's son.
fact: Its people speak a Berber language, not Arabic, at home.

clue: Two brothers and their surgeon father built a world-famous medical center in this city.
fact: The clinic grew after a deadly 1883 tornado hit the town.

clue: This small town in eastern Iowa calls itself the future birthplace of Captain James T. Kirk, who will be born there in 2228.
fact: A stone marks the exact future spot behind a barbershop.

clue: Most of the world's rough diamonds pass through a few blocks of this Belgian port.
fact: The painter Rubens's house and studio there is a museum.

clue: Surrounded during the Battle of the Bulge, an American general here answered the German surrender demand with one word: "Nuts!"
fact: Patton's Third Army broke through to the town on December 26, 1944.

clue: Founded in 670, this was the first great Muslim city in North Africa, and its Great Mosque is one of the oldest in the world.
fact: It is called the fourth holiest city in Islam.

clue: A 120-foot steel baseball bat leans against the museum and factory of a famous bat maker in this city.
fact: The first bat was reportedly made in 1884 for a slumping local player.

clue: Mormon founder Joseph Smith was killed by a mob that stormed the jail in this town in 1844.
fact: His followers soon left nearby Nauvoo and headed west under Brigham Young.

clue: Australia's third-largest city, on a winding river in Queensland, will host the 2032 Summer Olympics.
fact: Lone Pine Koala Sanctuary there, open since 1927, is the world's oldest koala sanctuary.

clue: An eight-story garment factory building collapsed outside this capital in April 2013, killing more than 1,100 workers.
fact: Workers had been ordered back inside a day after cracks appeared in the walls.

clue: This city became its country's capital in 1923, replacing a far larger city on the Bosphorus; Angora cats and goats are named after it.
fact: Atatürk's mausoleum, Anıtkabir, stands on a hill here.

clue: Fracking in the Bakken shale turned this town into an oil boomtown around 2010, with workers sleeping in their trucks.
fact: At the peak, Walmart parking lots there filled up with campers.

clue: Visitors to this state park in southwestern Arkansas can dig in a plowed field for diamonds and keep what they find.
answer: Crater of Diamonds State Park, Arkansas
fact: The largest diamond found there weighed 40.23 carats, in 1924.

clue: Pastel houses climb the steep hills of this Pacific port, linked to the harbor by more than a dozen old funicular elevators.
fact: Poet Pablo Neruda had a house there called La Sebastiana.

clue: A Muisca chief covered in gold dust dove into this round lake as an offering, starting the legend of El Dorado.
fact: A 1580s attempt to drain it cut a notch in its rim that can still be seen.

clue: The Library of Ashurbanipal, which held the Epic of Gilgamesh, was dug out of the ruins of this Assyrian capital.
fact: ISIS destroyed some of its gates in 2016.

clue: A Mexican-themed rest stop with a giant sombrero tower sits just south of the North Carolina line here; billboards for it run for hundreds of miles.
answer: South of the Border, Dillon, South Carolina
fact: Its mascot is a cartoon named Pedro.

clue: The Comstock Lode, a huge silver strike, built this mountain boomtown in 1859, and Mark Twain first used his pen name at its newspaper.
fact: Silver from the Comstock helped pay for the Union in the Civil War.

clue: A Roman city of columned streets, an oval plaza and theaters, just north of Amman, is so well preserved it is called the "Pompeii of the East."
fact: It hosts a summer festival of music and dance among the ruins.

clue: British troops took thousands of brass plaques and sculptures from this royal city in 1897; museums are now returning some.
fact: The Benin Bronzes were made using the lost-wax casting method.

clue: More than 1,200 stone steps climb through the jungle to the terraces of this Tayrona city, which was rediscovered by looters in 1972.
fact: The city is several hundred years older than Machu Picchu.

clue: The Kennedy family has summered at its oceanfront compound in this Cape Cod village since the 1920s.
fact: JFK used the compound as his summer White House.

clue: A colony's first settlers landed here in 1634, and its assembly passed one of the first laws granting religious toleration in the colonies in 1649.
fact: It was Maryland's capital until 1695, when the capital moved to Annapolis.

clue: Elephants used to carry tourists up the ramp to this honey-colored hilltop fort-palace outside the "Pink City."
fact: Its Sheesh Mahal hall is covered in tiny mirrors that glitter in candlelight.

clue: French Revolutionary troops stopped the Prussians with an artillery duel at this windmill in September 1792; Goethe said a new era began.
fact: The French declared the First Republic the next day.

clue: Airbus assembles its jets in this pink-brick French city, nicknamed "La Ville Rose."
fact: It is also home to Europe's biggest space center.

clue: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline begins its 800-mile run south at the oil fields of this Arctic bay.
fact: It was the largest oil field ever found in North America.

clue: The National Security Agency's headquarters is at an Army base here, between Baltimore and Washington.
fact: The NSA was so secret people joked its initials meant "No Such Agency."

clue: Thousands of sandstone pillars rising out of the mist in this national park inspired the floating mountains in the movie Avatar.
fact: A glass-bottomed bridge there spans a canyon about 1,000 feet deep.

clue: Commandos blew up a heavy-water plant here in 1943 to slow Nazi atomic research.
fact: The town once built giant mirrors to bounce sunlight into its dark valley in winter.

clue: People lived in caves carved into a ravine here until the 1950s; the cave districts are now hotels and appeared in a James Bond chase.
fact: It was a European Capital of Culture in 2019.

clue: Visitors scramble up a steep "Dune Climb" at this Lake Michigan lakeshore, named for an Ojibwe legend of a mother bear.
fact: In the legend, her two cubs became the Manitou Islands.

clue: Washington Irving set his tale of a headless horseman and Ichabod Crane in this Hudson Valley village.
fact: Irving is buried in the village's cemetery.

clue: The Museum of Broken Relationships, full of objects left over from breakups, began in this Central European capital.
fact: A cannon in its upper town fires at noon every day.

clue: Architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed the School of Art in this city; it burned in 2014 and again in 2018.
fact: It is Scotland's largest city.

clue: U.S. Marines landed on this island in August 1942 and fought for six months to hold its airfield.
fact: The airfield was named Henderson Field after a Marine pilot killed at Midway.

clue: More than 107,000 fans fill the stadium called "the Big House" in this college town.
fact: It is the largest stadium in the United States.

clue: Blues guitarist B.B. King, whose guitar was named Lucille, grew up near this Delta town, now home to his museum.
fact: He named the guitar after a woman two men were fighting over when they started a fire at a dance.

clue: Africa's second-highest mountain stands almost on the equator and gave its name to the country around it.
fact: Its glaciers are shrinking fast.

clue: Edmund Hillary practiced climbing on this country's highest peak before Everest.
fact: Its summit lost about 33 feet in a 1991 rockslide.

clue: Christopher Columbus was born in this port, which has one of Europe's largest medieval old towns.
fact: Pesto comes from its region, Liguria.

clue: This 14,410-foot volcano towers over Seattle on a clear day and has the most glaciers of any peak in the lower 48.
fact: It is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world because of its mudflow risk.

clue: Young farm women known as "mill girls" ran the looms in this planned 1820s textile city on the Merrimack River.
fact: They published their own literary magazine, the Lowell Offering.

clue: About 100,000 fans can fill the cricket ground in this Australian city, which also hosts the Australian Open tennis.
fact: It was the national capital from 1901 to 1927.

clue: Oman's capital is home to a grand mosque, finished in 2001, with one of the world's largest chandeliers.
fact: Its prayer hall carpet was hand-woven by about 600 women.

clue: Henry IV signed an edict in this city in 1598 giving French Protestants religious freedom; Louis XIV revoked it in 1685.
fact: Many Huguenots fled abroad, to Prussia, England, the Netherlands and America.

clue: Country music theaters line the main strip of this Ozarks town, which has more theater seats than Broadway.
fact: The town first grew because of a 1907 novel, The Shepherd of the Hills.

clue: Aretha Franklin cut hits at FAME Studios here, and the Rolling Stones recorded "Brown Sugar" at a rival studio nearby started by FAME's own session players.
fact: Its studio musicians were known as "the Swampers."

clue: The world's largest lizards live on this island and its neighbors.
fact: The dragons can grow to 10 feet long.

clue: This dam on the Paraná River, shared by two countries, was the world's top producer of hydroelectric power for years.
fact: It supplies most of Paraguay's electricity.

clue: The last capital of the Western Roman Empire is famous for its glittering Byzantine mosaics of Justinian and Theodora.
fact: Dante is buried there.

clue: A life-size cow sculpted out of butter is the star attraction at this state fair.
fact: It takes about 600 pounds of butter.

clue: The eye of Hurricane Katrina came ashore near this Gulf Coast town in August 2005.
fact: Katrina's storm surge there was close to 30 feet.

clue: A statue of the Virgin Mary stands on Cerro San Cristóbal, a hill rising above this Andean capital.
fact: Snowcapped Andes rise just east of the city.

clue: Hernán Cortés landed and founded a town here in 1519; U.S. forces landed here in 1847 and occupied it again in 1914.
fact: Cortés is said to have scuttled his ships so his men couldn't turn back.

clue: The world's largest mud-brick building, a mosque in Mali's inland Niger delta rebuilt in 1907, is re-plastered by the whole town every year.
fact: Wooden beams stick out of the walls to hold up workers during re-plastering.

clue: Costumed interpreters bring a colony's 18th-century capital back to life in this restored town.
fact: John D. Rockefeller Jr. paid for much of the restoration.

clue: A 1930s stone and timber lodge on the slopes of Oregon's highest peak was used for the exterior shots of The Shining.
fact: It was built by the Works Progress Administration.

clue: A 17th-century Swedish warship that sank on its maiden voyage was raised and is displayed nearly intact in this capital's museum.
fact: The Vasa sank less than a mile into its first voyage in 1628.

clue: This city's medieval citadel stands on a mound in the center of one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, badly damaged in a 2010s war.
fact: Its covered souk was one of the largest in the world before the war.

clue: Archaeologists opened an unlooted royal tomb here in 1977, probably that of Alexander the Great's father, and found a gold chest marked with a sunburst.
fact: The sunburst symbol later figured in a long dispute over a neighboring country's name.

clue: Thousands of retired military planes are parked in rows in the desert at an Air Force base in this city, known as "the Boneyard."
fact: The dry air and hard ground keep the planes from rusting or sinking.

clue: Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of a stone arch at the north entrance to the first national park here.
fact: It says "For the Benefit and Enjoyment of the People."

clue: Some of the tallest sand dunes in the world glow red in Namibia's Namib Desert here, around a white clay pan dotted with dead camelthorn trees.
fact: The trees at Deadvlei are about 900 years old and too dry to rot.

clue: American and Soviet troops met for the first time on the Elbe River here in April 1945.
fact: April 25 is remembered as "Elbe Day."

clue: Buddhist monks carved about 30 cave temples into a horseshoe-shaped cliff here starting in the 2nd century BC; a British hunter found them in 1819.
fact: Their wall paintings are some of the oldest surviving in India.

clue: Up to 1.5 million bats stream out from under the Congress Avenue Bridge on summer evenings in this state capital.
fact: Its unofficial motto is "Keep Austin Weird."

clue: Woody Guthrie wrote songs about this concrete dam on the Columbia River, one of the largest in the U.S.
fact: It is the largest power station in the U.S.

clue: Atatürk was born in this Greek port, whose seafront is marked by the White Tower.
fact: It is Greece's second-largest city.

clue: A team of U.S. part-timers beat England 1–0 in this city in South America's largest country in 1950, one of the biggest upsets in World Cup history.
fact: Some English papers reportedly thought the score was a typo.

clue: France set off 193 nuclear tests at this remote atoll and its neighbor from 1966 to 1996.
fact: Protests over the last tests in 1995 included a boycott of French wine.

clue: Two friends started an ice cream company in a converted gas station in 1978; its factory and "Flavor Graveyard" are in this town.
fact: The friends learned to make ice cream from a $5 correspondence course.

clue: The "First Town in the First State" was started by Dutch settlers in 1631 near the mouth of a wide bay.
fact: Native people destroyed the first Dutch settlement within a year.

clue: This main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, built in 1395, sits in front of a mountain in the heart of a capital.
fact: Japan tore down most of its buildings during its colonial rule.

clue: The Greek fleet trapped and beat the much bigger Persian navy in the narrow strait by this island in 480 BC.
fact: Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore.

clue: Volvo was founded in this port, its country's second-largest city.
fact: Its Liseberg amusement park is one of the most visited in Scandinavia.

clue: The world's largest retailer started as Sam Walton's five-and-dime on the town square here.
fact: The original store is now a Walmart museum.

clue: Yale is in this city, and so is Louis' Lunch, which claims to have served America's first hamburger in 1900.
fact: Louis' Lunch still doesn't allow ketchup.

clue: An 18th-century bridge spans a 390-foot gorge splitting this clifftop town in Spain's Andalusia, a favorite of Hemingway and Orson Welles.
fact: It has one of the oldest bullrings in Spain.

clue: Oskar Schindler saved about 1,200 Jewish workers at his enamelware factory in this city.
fact: The factory is now a museum about the city under Nazi occupation.

clue: Alexander the Great beat Darius III's much larger army on a plain here in 331 BC, sealing the fall of the Persian Empire.
fact: Darius had the ground leveled so his scythed chariots could charge.

clue: White plank fences line the thoroughbred horse farms around this city, home of the Keeneland racecourse.
fact: It calls itself the "Horse Capital of the World."

clue: Bronner's, which bills itself as the world's largest Christmas store, is open 361 days a year in this Bavarian-style town in Michigan's Lower Peninsula.
fact: The town was founded by German Lutheran missionaries in 1845.

clue: The steel lattice "Bird's Nest" stadium hosted the opening ceremonies of two Olympic Games in this city.
fact: Beijing is the only city to have hosted both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

clue: Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín held their only meeting, behind closed doors, in this port city on South America's Pacific coast in 1822.
fact: No one knows exactly what they said; San Martín soon retired to Europe.

clue: Thousands of huge stone jars, some 10 feet tall and 2,000 years old, are scattered across a plateau, with the biggest group just outside this town; no one knows for sure what they were for.
fact: The area was one of the most heavily bombed places on Earth during the Vietnam War.

clue: Baseball's spring training and gangster Al Capone both came to this spa town's Bathhouse Row of hot springs.
fact: The hot springs were set aside by Congress in 1832, before Yellowstone existed.

clue: Thornton Wilder wrote much of Our Town at an artists' colony in this town, which is often said to be the model for Grover's Corners.
fact: The MacDowell artists' colony there was founded in 1907.

clue: Overwater bungalows ring the turquoise lagoon around Mount Otemanu on this island.
fact: The U.S. built a supply base there during World War II.

clue: Soviet irrigation projects shrank this once-huge lake so much that a fishing town now sits more than 60 miles from the water, with rusting ships in the sand.
fact: It was once the fourth-largest lake in the world.

clue: This Peruvian "White City" was built from pale volcanic stone beneath the volcano El Misti.
fact: The frozen Inca mummy "Juanita" is displayed in a museum there.

clue: The NASCAR Hall of Fame is in this city, which has a 1.5-mile speedway just outside it.
fact: Most NASCAR teams are based in the area.

clue: Lost luggage from the airlines ends up for sale at a huge store in this town.
fact: Staff have found an Egyptian burial mask and a camera from a NASA space shuttle in lost bags.

clue: Most of a country's wine comes from vineyards around this city at the foot of the Andes.
fact: Malbec grapes from France do especially well there.

clue: Ornate wooden houseboats line this lake in the Kashmir valley.
fact: Vendors sell flowers and vegetables from boats at a floating market there.

clue: Pirates made this harbor town the "wickedest city on Earth" until an earthquake sank much of it into the sea in 1692.
fact: Henry Morgan was based there.

clue: The U.S. Air Force Academy's aluminum-and-glass chapel, with 17 spires, stands on the edge of this city at the foot of the Rockies.
answer: U.S. Air Force Academy, Colorado Springs
fact: Pikes Peak rises just west of the city.

clue: F. Scott Fitzgerald was born in this state capital, the smaller of a pair of "Twin Cities" on the Mississippi.
fact: It holds a big Winter Carnival, sometimes with ice palaces.

clue: Giant sculptures of snow and ice fill Odori Park every February at this city's snow festival.
fact: The festival started in 1950 with six snow statues built by high school students.

clue: Sputnik, Yuri Gagarin and every Soyuz crew have launched from this spaceport, which Russia rents from its neighbor.
fact: Russia pays about $115 million a year to lease it.

clue: This hillside town has been the world's perfume capital since the 1700s; jasmine for a famous Chanel scent is still grown around it.
fact: It started as a leather-tanning town that perfumed its gloves.

clue: A giant carving of three Confederate leaders on horseback covers the side of this granite dome.
fact: The carving covers about three acres.

clue: National Guard troops attacked a tent colony of striking coal miners in southern Colorado here in 1914, killing about 20 people, including women and children.
fact: The United Mine Workers own the site and keep a memorial there.

clue: Thousands of glowworms light up the ceiling of a grotto in these caves on New Zealand's North Island, which visitors see from boats in the dark.
fact: The "glowworms" are actually fly larvae.

clue: Ferdinand Magellan was killed fighting the chief Lapulapu on this small island in 1521.
fact: Lapulapu is now a national hero, and his statue stands near the battle site.

clue: Johannes Gutenberg printed his Bible on a movable-type press in this Rhine city around 1455.
fact: A museum there named for him holds original copies of the Bible.

clue: The Ohio State Buckeyes play in a horseshoe-shaped stadium in this state capital, Ohio's largest city.
fact: The stadium seats more than 100,000 fans.

clue: Cell phones and Wi-Fi are restricted around this town because of the giant radio telescope there.
fact: The town is in the 13,000-square-mile National Radio Quiet Zone.

clue: The Ifugao people carved rice terraces into these mountainsides on Luzon, in the Philippines, by hand, centuries ago.
fact: They were long said to be 2,000 years old, but recent digs suggest most are only a few hundred years old.

clue: The "Battle of the Nations," the biggest European battle before World War I, defeated Napoleon outside this city in 1813.
fact: A huge stone monument there was finished on the 100th anniversary.

clue: This capital's old town sits on cliffs above deep river gorges, honeycombed with tunnels called casemates.
fact: Its country is the world's only grand duchy.

clue: Harry Truman's white Victorian home and presidential library are in this city, which was the starting point of the Oregon Trail.
fact: Truman hung a sign on his desk saying "The Buck Stops Here."

clue: A famous outdoor-gear company's flagship store in this town stays open all night, every night.
fact: The company's first product was a rubber-bottomed hunting boot in 1912.

clue: Frank Gehry's titanium-covered art museum turned this industrial city into a tourist magnet when it opened in 1997.
fact: Cities copying the effect is called the "Bilbao effect."

clue: The Prophet Muhammad is buried under the green dome of a mosque in this city.
fact: He moved there from Mecca in 622, which is year one of the Islamic calendar.

clue: Scotland's attempt to start a trading colony on this isthmus in 1698 failed so badly that it pushed the country into union with England.
fact: About a fifth of Scotland's money was invested in the scheme.

clue: Sand dunes rise along the southern shore of Lake Michigan in this national park, steel mills on either side.
fact: It became a national park in 2019.

clue: A fur-trading post that became an Army fort was a key stop for pioneers on the Oregon Trail here.
fact: Big treaties with the Plains tribes were signed there in 1851 and 1868.

clue: IDES OF MARCH: Julius Caesar was stabbed to death on March 15, 44 BC, in a meeting hall next to Pompey's theater, whose ruins are now a sunken square full of cats.
fact: A cat shelter operates in the ruins.

clue: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498 near this port on the Malabar Coast, opening a sea route from Europe.
fact: The cotton cloth calico is named after the city.

clue: Chile took this port city from Bolivia in the War of the Pacific, leaving Bolivia without a coastline.
fact: Bolivia still has a navy, which trains on Lake Titicaca.

clue: Several steps of this state capitol carry markers claiming to be exactly one mile above sea level, from surveys made over more than a century.
fact: A new marker, from a 2026 survey, was added on the 17th step.

clue: The oldest continuous Fourth of July celebration in the U.S. has been held in this harbor town on Narragansett Bay since 1785.
fact: A red, white and blue line is painted down the parade route.

clue: Moses is said to have looked out over the Promised Land from this Jordanian peak before he died.
fact: Pope John Paul II visited it in 2000.

clue: U.S. soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed villagers in this hamlet on March 16, 1968.
fact: Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson landed between the soldiers and villagers to stop the killing.

clue: Saddam Hussein's forces attacked this town with chemical weapons on March 16, 1988, killing thousands of civilians.
fact: It was the deadliest chemical attack on civilians in history.

clue: ST. PATRICK'S DAY: The biggest St. Patrick's Day parade in the world, first held in 1762, marches up Fifth Avenue past this Gothic cathedral.
answer: St. Patrick's Cathedral, New York City
fact: The parade still doesn't allow cars or floats.

clue: ST. PATRICK'S DAY: This Route 66 town in the Texas Panhandle, named for an Irish symbol, holds a big St. Patrick's celebration.
fact: Its Art Deco U-Drop Inn inspired a building in the movie Cars.

clue: ST. PATRICK'S DAY: Legend says St. Patrick converted the King of Munster on this rocky hilltop, crowned with a medieval cathedral and round tower.
fact: Queen Elizabeth II visited it in 2011.

clue: ST. PATRICK'S DAY: St. Patrick is said to be buried in the churchyard of the cathedral in this town.
fact: A big granite stone marks the grave.

clue: ST. PATRICK'S DAY: Thousands of pilgrims, some barefoot, climb this mountain where St. Patrick is said to have fasted for 40 days.
fact: The pilgrimage is held on the last Sunday in July.

clue: A 15-foot statue of Superman stands in the town square of this Ohio River town at the southern tip of Illinois, which calls itself his official hometown.
fact: It holds a Superman Celebration every June.

clue: A huge gold mine that operated until 2002 now holds a physics lab deep underground for catching neutrinos.
fact: It was the largest and deepest gold mine in North America.

clue: Pastel houses cascade down the cliffs of this town on the Amalfi Coast.
fact: John Steinbeck wrote that it "bites deep."

clue: Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians all make pilgrimages to a "footprint" on top of this mountain.
fact: Pilgrims usually climb at night to see the sunrise from the summit.

clue: The ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire's capital lie among huge piles of boulders here; it was sacked in 1565.
fact: Portuguese visitors compared the city to Rome.

clue: The Apollo 13 command module is on display at a space museum in this central Kansas town.
fact: It has one of the largest collections of U.S. and Soviet space artifacts in the world.

clue: Thousands camped near this reservation in 2016 to protest the Dakota Access Pipeline's crossing near the Missouri River.
fact: Sitting Bull lived on the reservation and was killed there in 1890.

clue: This white wooden castle, nicknamed "White Heron Castle," is the finest surviving Japanese castle.
fact: It survived Allied bombing in World War II.

clue: A Dutch-built sea fort encloses the old town of this port near Sri Lanka's southern tip.
fact: Its walls shielded much of the old town from the 2004 tsunami.

clue: A huge Sunday livestock bazaar has drawn traders for centuries to this Silk Road oasis in Xinjiang, near China's borders with Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
fact: Many locals keep unofficial time two hours behind Beijing.

clue: This secret city was built in 1942 to enrich uranium for the atomic bomb; it didn't appear on maps.
fact: Its population went from about 3,000 to 75,000 in three years.

clue: A 306-foot stone obelisk honors a 1777 Revolutionary War battle that was actually fought a few miles away in New York.
fact: It is the tallest structure in Vermont.

clue: One of the world's highest active volcanoes, this nearly perfect snow-capped cone in the Andes overlooks a capital that sits almost on the equator.
fact: It is 19,347 feet tall.

clue: The world's largest Buddhist temple, a huge stepped stupa with 504 Buddha statues, was buried in volcanic ash here for centuries.
fact: Its walls are covered with 2,672 carved relief panels.

clue: For about 6,000 years, Plains hunters stampeded bison over a cliff here in the foothills of the Rockies.
fact: The name comes from a legend of a young man crushed while watching from below the cliff.

clue: Albert Einstein lived in this college town for the last 22 years of his life.
fact: His brain was taken during the autopsy without his family's permission.

clue: An organ built in these caverns plays music by tapping stalactites with rubber mallets.
fact: Building the Great Stalacpipe Organ took three years.

clue: This white marble mosque, one of the largest in the world, has 82 domes and was finished in 2007 in this Gulf capital.
answer: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, Abu Dhabi
fact: It has one of the largest hand-knotted carpets in the world.

clue: The tomb of a Maya king named Pakal was found deep inside a pyramid at this jungle city in 1952.
fact: His sarcophagus lid shows him falling into the underworld.

clue: A Russian prince beat the Mongol Golden Horde at this field in 1380, the first major Russian victory against them.
fact: The prince, Dmitry, was afterward called "Donskoy," for the Don River.

clue: The Negro Leagues Baseball Museum is at 18th and Vine, the historic jazz district of this city.
fact: The Negro National League was founded there in 1920.

clue: The 17-mile Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel starts at the edge of this resort city.
fact: It is the most populous city in its state.

clue: Chocolate shops and ski slopes fill this Swiss-style town on a big lake in the Patagonian Andes of Argentina.
fact: It was settled largely by Swiss, German and Austrian immigrants.

clue: The deep "blue" of this Gothic cathedral's 12th- and 13th-century stained glass is famous, and so is the labyrinth on its floor.
fact: Its two spires don't match because they were built centuries apart.

clue: Builders of this pre-Inca city near the world's highest navigable lake carved a monolithic stone doorway called the Gateway of the Sun.
fact: It may have had more than 20,000 residents around AD 800.
